flashcards.q: Why is parameterization structurally complete while escaping is not?
flashcards.a: Parameterization compiles the query's STRUCTURE first, then binds values through a separate channel the parser never re-interprets as syntax -- no code path lets a value alter structure. Escaping patches the SAME channel as syntax and is only as complete as its author's anticipation of every dangerous sequence (real historical bypasses exist, e.g. MySQL multi-byte charset tricks defeating naive backslash-escaping).

flashcards.q: How many requests does boolean-blind extraction of a 32-character password hash typically require, and why?
flashcards.a: ~224 requests. Binary search over the printable ASCII range (~95 values) needs ceil(log2(95)) ~ 7 requests per character via true/false narrowing, so 32 characters x 7 ~ 224 total -- this is what sqlmap automates.

flashcards.q: When is time-blind SQL injection used instead of boolean-blind, and what's its main cost?
flashcards.a: Used when even a behavioral true/false difference isn't observable -- infer truth from response latency via IF(condition, SLEEP(5), SLEEP(0)) instead of content. Dramatically slower since each query requires waiting out a real delay; also more detectable via anomalous latency patterns.

flashcards.q: What makes second-order SQL injection uniquely hard to catch via code review or scanning?
flashcards.a: The payload is stored via a correctly parameterized write (genuinely safe at that point) and only becomes exploitable later when a DIFFERENT code path reads it back and uses it to build a different, often unparameterized query. A reviewer checking the write path finds nothing wrong -- the vulnerability lives entirely in an unrelated read-then-query path elsewhere.

flashcards.q: What is out-of-band SQL injection and when is it used?
flashcards.a: Used when neither response content nor timing gives usable signal (heavily filtered/async environments). The database itself is made to initiate an outbound DNS or HTTP request (xp_dirtree DNS lookup, Oracle UTL_HTTP) encoding exfiltrated data into that request, logged on attacker-controlled infrastructure.

flashcards.q: Where does SQL injection still live in a codebase that 'uses an ORM'?
flashcards.a: In the ORM's raw-SQL escape hatches (.raw()/.extra()/text()/find_by_sql with concatenated input), and in dynamic identifier construction (table/column names, sort direction) -- parameterization binds VALUES not identifiers, so these need an explicit allowlist, never interpolation.

flashcards.q: Explain the NoSQL operator-injection authentication bypass.
flashcards.a: If a client-supplied value is passed directly into a query position without type validation, sending {"password": {"$ne": null}} makes MongoDB interpret $ne as an operator ('not equal to null'), true for any non-null password -- bypassing authentication with zero password guessing. Fix: validate that user-supplied values are the expected plain scalar type before querying.

flashcards.q: What is the unifying fix pattern across command injection, LDAP injection, and SSTI?
flashcards.a: Same structural bug as SQLi (untrusted data interpreted as syntax by an interpreter). Fix: use each interpreter's own value-binding mechanism -- exec with an argument list (never shell=True) for commands, the LDAP library's escape API for filters, and template CONTEXT DATA (never concatenation into template SOURCE) for SSTI.

flashcards.q: Why does prompt injection have no fix analogous to parameterized queries?
flashcards.a: SQL has a formal grammar letting a parser mechanically enforce 'this slot is a value, never re-parsed as syntax.' Natural language has no equivalent grammar -- there's no token that reliably marks 'data, not instruction,' and the model is trained to follow instructions wherever they appear in its input.

flashcards.q: What is indirect prompt injection and why is it harder to defend than direct injection?
flashcards.a: The malicious instruction arrives embedded in content the model processes on the system's behalf (a retrieved document, webpage, tool output) rather than from the end user directly -- traditional 'validate user input' thinking doesn't cover it since the input isn't from the user at all.

flashcards.q: Which prompt injection mitigation is closest to 'structural' and why?
flashcards.a: Privilege separation of agent tools -- it doesn't try to detect or prevent the injection itself, it bounds the CONSEQUENCE regardless of whether the model was successfully manipulated (e.g. a summarization agent has no tool that can query arbitrary tables or send emails). This is a fundamentally more robust guarantee than any detection-based mitigation (provenance marking, classifiers), which remain probabilistic and evadable.

flashcards.q: What is prompt injection's rank in OWASP's LLM Top 10, and for how long?
flashcards.a: Ranked the #1 risk (LLM01) for two consecutive editions as of 2025, reflecting that the underlying architectural gap -- instructions and data sharing one undifferentiated channel -- remains unsolved.
